newsitem.title: UK: Britain names dates for Scottish, Welsh polls.
newsitem.headline: Britain names dates for Scottish, Welsh polls.

text.p: The Labour government confirmed its commitment to a radical shake-up of Britain's constitution on Thursday by naming the date for referendums in Scotland and Wales on plans to give the two nations their own parliaments.
In a further sign of readiness to make changes, the cabinet also agreed that voters would in future choose British members of the European Parliament by proportional representation (PR).
Scottish Secretary Donald Dewar said the plebiscite which is almost certain to give Scotland its first parliament since the 1707 Act of Union with England will take place on September 11.
A similar poll on the setting up of a Welsh senate will take place a week later.

The plans for so-called "devolution" were a key issue in Britain's May 1 election, with the Conservatives warning that Labour's plans were the first step on a slippery slope towards the break-up of Britain.
But electors in the two countries involved showed their disdain for these warnings, and not a single Conservative was returned to parliament for a Scottish or a Welsh seat.
Scottish voters will be asked in September to endorse the government's plans for the new parliament to control most of Scotland's internal affairs.
A separate question on the voting paper will ask them to approve powers for the parliament to vary the rate of income tax by up to three pence in the pound from the level prevailing in England.

Meanwhile, Home Secretary Jack Straw, Britain's interior minister, announced that legislation will be introduced soon to allow all Britain's 87 members of the European Parliament to be chosen by a PR system for the first time in 1999.

Britain is at present the odd member state out in the European Union in electing most of its MEPs by a first-past-the-post system, although the three Northern Irish members have always been elected by PR.
First-past-the-post gives larger parties a big advantage, and helped Labour to win 62 seats at the last European parliament elections in 1994.

Straw, who personally believes first-past-the-post has advantages in producing strong one-party governments, denied that this reform was setting Britain on another slippery slope -- towards PR for the British parliament.
"The European Parliament is not an executive body, so arguments about strong government, weak government do not arise. It is a representative body," Straw said.
